```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
set.seed(1)
```

## Why a Measurement Package Owes You Evidence

A package that reports reliability, fit, and validity coefficients is
asking you to put those numbers in a manuscript. Assurance that the
numbers are right is worth very little; evidence that they are right,
which you can re-run on your own machine, is worth a great deal. This
vignette is that evidence. Nothing in it is transcribed from a previous
run: every number below is computed when the vignette is built, so if a
claim were to stop being true the vignette would say so.

The claim to verify comes in two parts. Most estimation and inference
come from DMAR (every exploratory factor analysis, the EFA page's, the
Items page's live EFA and the solutions behind VSS and the Optimizer's
simple structure, and the Dimensionality page's parallel analysis among
them), the fitting from lavaan (Rosseel, 2012), and the polychoric,
tetrachoric and mixed correlations from psych; for
those, SIEVER's job is to route your data to the right routine with the
right arguments, to gate the analyses that are not yet estimable, and to
record what it did, so what can go wrong is the routing. The counted
percentile bootstrap of robust omega for independent rows is DMAR's
(DMAR 1.1.0), so for it SIEVER's part is the request and its record.
SIEVER also has procedures of its own (among them the whole-cluster
counted bootstrap of reliability under a declared cluster design, the
response screens, the composite and factor score records, and the Monte
Carlo intervals), whose arithmetic is its own to get right. The checks
below say which kind each one is: a quantity
compared with a derivation written out in the open is checked apart from
the engine, while a quantity compared with the same engine reached
another way checks the routing, not the estimator.

Three kinds of evidence appear here.

1. **Agreement with authoritative sources.** Each quantity checked below
   is reproduced from a second implementation (lavaan) or from a
   derivation written out in the open, item by item. These are checks of
   those quantities on these data, not of every number SIEVER displays.
2. **Invariants that must hold for every input.** Some properties follow
   from how a procedure is built, whatever the data (an interval built
   around one estimate with one standard error widens with its confidence
   level; reverse coding applied twice returns the original values).
   Checks of this kind, called metamorphic tests, catch defects that a
   single fixed comparison can miss.
3. **Reproducibility.** A seeded computation must give the same answer
   twice, and it must leave your random number stream exactly as it found
   it.

Where two respectable definitions disagree, this vignette shows both
and explains the disagreement rather than choosing the flattering one.
Three such cases appear below (Harman's screen, HTMT and AVE) and none is
an error: they are definitional differences that a user needs to know
about to report the right thing.

## The Data and the Model

The running example is the Holzinger and Swineford (1939) primary nine
mental tests (n = 301), shipped in DMAR as `holzinger_swineford`, with the three
theorized ability factors Visual, Textual, and Speed. SIEVER carries the
same nine tests as its default bundled example (through an internal
fixture), but the code below uses `DMAR::holzinger_swineford` directly so that
everything you copy from this page runs outside the app.

```{r data}
library(DMAR)
library(lavaan)

items <- c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges",
           "t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence", "t9_word_meaning",
           "t10_addition", "t12_counting_groups_of_dots",
           "t13_straight_and_curved_capitals")
d <- holzinger_swineford[, items]
blocks <- list(Visual  = items[1:3],
               Textual = items[4:6],
               Speed   = items[7:9])

model <- '
  Visual  =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges
  Textual =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning
  Speed   =~ t10_addition + t12_counting_groups_of_dots + t13_straight_and_curved_capitals
'
fit <- cfa(model, data = d, std.lv = TRUE)
c(n = nobs(fit), items = length(items))
```

The measurement model fixes the factor variances to one (`std.lv = TRUE`),
the SIEVER default and the identification the derivations below assume:
every loading is free and the factors are on a standardized scale, while
the items keep their own scales (lavaan's Std.lv solution). The completely
standardized solution (Std.all), which rescales the items as well, is a
separate output.

## Agreement With Authoritative Sources

### ECVI: DMAR Versus lavaan

The expected cross validation index (Browne & Cudeck, 1989) is a
discrepancy per observation, so it is on an interpretable metric and takes
a confidence interval, which is why SIEVER reports it, with its interval,
beside CFI, RMSEA, and SRMR on the CV and Invariance tab (the calibration
and validation rows and the invariance ladder). lavaan computes the point
estimate as a fit
measure; DMAR computes the same point estimate and adds the noncentral
chi square interval that lavaan does not provide. The point estimates must
be identical.

```{r ecvi}
e_dmar   <- ecvi(fit)
e_lavaan <- unname(fitMeasures(fit, "ecvi"))

sprintf("DMAR::ecvi()          %.12f", e_dmar$value[e_dmar$term == "ecvi"])
sprintf("lavaan fitMeasures()  %.12f", e_lavaan)
sprintf("absolute difference   %.3e",
        abs(e_dmar$value[e_dmar$term == "ecvi"] - e_lavaan))
```

The absolute difference is at or below the resolution of double precision
arithmetic (it prints as exactly zero here), so the agreement runs well
past the twelve digits shown. What DMAR adds is the interval:

```{r ecvi-interval}
e_dmar
```

### Robust Omega: DMAR Versus a Hand Derivation

The Reliability tab's default coefficient is Robust omega (observed
denominator), the coefficient Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016)
introduced as hierarchical omega: the squared sum of the one-factor
loadings over the variance of the unit-weighted composite, with that
variance estimated from the data rather than from the model. Writing
`lambda` for the loadings of the one-factor model with the factor variance
fixed to one, `psi` for its residual variances, and `S` for the
unrestricted covariance matrix of the items on the maximum likelihood
divisor (n, the divisor the loadings were estimated under):

```
  robust omega         = sum(lambda)^2 / sum(S)
  model-implied omega  = sum(lambda)^2 / (sum(lambda)^2 + sum(psi))
```

The numerator is the same under both; only the denominator differs, and
the two denominators differ by exactly `sum(S - Sigma_hat)`, the sum of
every residual covariance of the one-factor fit. For a construct of three
items the one-factor model is saturated, so the residuals are zero (to the
optimizer's convergence tolerance) and the two coincide; the nine tests
forced into one factor, a model that is wrong
by construction, show the two parting company by exactly that sum. Both
rows are computed by `DMAR::reliability_omega()` and by hand from the same
lavaan fit.

```{r robust-omega}
omega_by_hand <- function(X) {
  fit1 <- cfa(paste("f =~", paste(names(X), collapse = " + ")),
              data = X, std.lv = TRUE)
  est <- lavInspect(fit1, "est")
  lambda <- est$lambda[, 1]
  psi <- diag(est$theta)
  S <- cov(X) * (nrow(X) - 1) / nrow(X)
  Sigma_hat <- lavInspect(fit1, "implied")$cov
  c(robust = sum(lambda)^2 / sum(S),
    model_implied = sum(lambda)^2 / (sum(lambda)^2 + sum(psi)),
    residual_sum = sum(S - Sigma_hat))
}
omega_dmar <- function(X) {
  value <- function(denominator) {
    r <- reliability_omega(data = X, denominator = denominator, ci_method = "none")
    r$value[r$term == "estimate"]
  }
  c(robust = value("observed"), model_implied = value("model_implied"))
}

sets <- list(Textual_three_items = d[, blocks$Textual], nine_tests_one_factor = d)
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sets), function(nm) {
  hand <- omega_by_hand(sets[[nm]])
  dmar <- omega_dmar(sets[[nm]])
  data.frame(items = nm,
             DMAR_robust = dmar[["robust"]], hand_robust = hand[["robust"]],
             DMAR_model_implied = dmar[["model_implied"]],
             hand_model_implied = hand[["model_implied"]],
             max_abs_difference = max(abs(dmar - hand[c("robust", "model_implied")])),
             residual_sum = hand[["residual_sum"]])
}))
```

DMAR and the hand derivation agree to machine precision on both rows, and
the residual sum is zero to the optimizer's convergence tolerance (about
1e-8 here) where the model is saturated and far from zero where it is
wrong. The second row is not a reliability anyone should
report (nine tests on different metrics are not one composite); it is here
because it is the case in which the choice of denominator matters, and it
shows what the choice is: the model-implied form describes the composite
as the fitted model describes it, and the robust form describes the
composite users compute. The interval SIEVER attaches to robust omega is a
percentile bootstrap (BCa for ordered items), run on request with its
wait stated, which is why the comparison here is of point estimates.

### Bifactor Indices: DMAR Versus a Hand Derivation

No second package is needed here, because the bifactor indices
(Rodriguez, Reise, & Haviland, 2016) are functions of the standardized
solution and can be derived in the open. Fit
the bifactor model (one general factor on all nine tests, three orthogonal
group factors), then compute the indices twice: once with
`DMAR::bifactor_indices()` and once from the standardized loadings, using
the definitions written out below.

Writing `g[i]` for the general loading of item `i`, `s[i]` for its group
factor loading, and `theta[i] = 1 - g[i]^2 - s[i]^2` for its standardized
residual variance:

```
  ECV     = sum(g^2) / (sum(g^2) + sum(s^2))
  omega   = (G + S) / (G + S + sum(theta))
  omega_H =  G      / (G + S + sum(theta))
            where G = sum(g)^2  and  S = sum over group factors of
            (sum of that factor's s)^2
  H       = t / (1 + t),  t = sum(g^2 / (1 - g^2))     (Hancock & Mueller, 2001)
```

The form of `H` matters. Coefficient H is the squared correlation between
the factor and its optimally weighted composite, and the Hancock and
Mueller (2001) expression above is what it is; a superficially similar
expression built from `sum(g^2)` alone is a different quantity, and such
a variant is exactly what this comparison exists to catch.

```{r bifactor}
bimodel <- '
  g       =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges +
             t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning +
             t10_addition + t12_counting_groups_of_dots +
             t13_straight_and_curved_capitals
  Visual  =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges
  Textual =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning
  Speed   =~ t10_addition + t12_counting_groups_of_dots + t13_straight_and_curved_capitals
'
bifit <- cfa(bimodel, data = d, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
bi <- bifactor_indices(bifit)
bi
```

Now the same four quantities for the general factor, by hand:

```{r bifactor-hand}
std <- standardizedSolution(bifit)
lam <- std[std$op == "=~", ]

g <- setNames(lam$est.std[lam$lhs == "g"], lam$rhs[lam$lhs == "g"])[items]
s <- unlist(lapply(names(blocks), function(b)
  setNames(lam$est.std[lam$lhs == b], lam$rhs[lam$lhs == b])))[items]
theta <- 1 - g^2 - s^2
grp <- rep(names(blocks), lengths(blocks))

G <- sum(g)^2
S <- sum(tapply(s, grp, function(x) sum(x)^2))
tt <- sum(g^2 / (1 - g^2))

hand <- c(ECV     = sum(g^2) / (sum(g^2) + sum(s^2)),
          omega   = (G + S) / (G + S + sum(theta)),
          omega_H = G / (G + S + sum(theta)),
          H       = tt / (1 + tt))
dmar <- unlist(bi[bi$factor == "g", names(hand)])

data.frame(index = names(hand),
           hand = unname(hand),
           DMAR = unname(dmar),
           abs_difference = unname(abs(hand - dmar)))
```

Every difference is zero to machine precision.

This model is also a useful reminder that agreement is not the same as
trustworthiness. The nine test bifactor solution is improper on this data
(a negative residual variance), which lavaan's post-estimation check and
DMAR both report as warnings above, and DMAR records on the result:

```{r bifactor-improper}
attr(bi, "improper")
```

SIEVER surfaces that flag rather than quietly printing the indices, since
indices from a Heywood solution should not be interpreted. The arithmetic
check is unaffected, because both routes read the same standardized
solution; what the flag says is that the solution itself needs
respecification before the numbers mean anything.

### The Harman Single Factor Screen

The Harman screen is the crudest common method variance diagnostic
(Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003): the share of the total
item variance that one common factor accounts for. It is a screen, not a
test, and SIEVER's Validity tab names it Harman's single-factor screen in
its table row, note, and button, and reports the proportion without a
cutoff; the note names the .50 convention of Podsakoff et al. (2003) once
and says that SIEVER applies no cutoff to it. Its
definition is where implementations part company, and SIEVER's note on
the Validity tab says which one it reports: as DMAR computes it, one
common factor is fit by maximum likelihood (`stats::factanal()`) to the
Pearson correlation matrix of the included items on the pairwise complete
cases, and the statistic is the sum of the squared standardized loadings
over the number of items. The other form in circulation divides the
largest eigenvalue of the correlation matrix by the number of items, which
is the variance of the first principal component, not of a factor: a
component absorbs unique as well as common variance, so that form
overstates the share and is not what SIEVER reports. Both are computed
below.

```{r harman}
h <- common_method_single_factor(d)
R <- cor(d, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
one_factor <- stats::factanal(covmat = R, factors = 1L)
factor_by_hand <- sum(one_factor$loadings[, 1]^2) / ncol(R)
component_form <- max(eigen(R, only.values = TRUE)$values) / ncol(R)

sprintf("DMAR::common_method_single_factor()        %.12f",
        h$value[h$term == "variance_explained"])
sprintf("one-factor ML loadings: sum(L^2) / p     %.12f", factor_by_hand)
sprintf("absolute difference                      %.3e",
        abs(h$value[h$term == "variance_explained"] - factor_by_hand))
sprintf("largest eigenvalue / p (component form)  %.12f", component_form)
```

DMAR and the one-factor derivation are identical to the printed
resolution, which is what a one line routing wrapper should deliver, and
the component form is visibly larger on the same matrix. A reader
comparing SIEVER's screen with a value from software that reports the
component form should expect the difference, and a .50 rule can land on
opposite sides of it.

### HTMT: DMAR Versus a Hand Derivation, and Why the Variants Differ

The heterotrait monotrait ratio (Henseler, Ringle, & Sarstedt, 2015)
compares the average between construct item correlation to the geometric
mean of the two constructs' average within construct item correlations.
DMAR implements this original arithmetic mean form, which is the form
SIEVER displays (the Validity tab names the routine, DMAR::htmt on each
construct's items, at the point of display). A
later variant (HTMT2), proposed for congeneric measures, replaces the
arithmetic means with geometric means, and some software now reports it
by default; on the same data it gives different values. Both are computed
by hand below from the item correlation matrix, so the column that DMAR
matches settles which definition it implements.

```{r htmt}
ht <- htmt(d, blocks = blocks)

R <- abs(cor(d))
htmt_by_hand <- function(a, b, average) {
  within <- function(ix) {
    r <- R[ix, ix]
    average(r[lower.tri(r)])
  }
  average(R[blocks[[a]], blocks[[b]]]) /
    sqrt(within(blocks[[a]]) * within(blocks[[b]]))
}
geometric <- function(v) exp(mean(log(v)))
arithmetic_by_hand <- mapply(htmt_by_hand, ht$construct_1, ht$construct_2,
                             MoreArgs = list(average = mean))
geometric_HTMT2 <- mapply(htmt_by_hand, ht$construct_1, ht$construct_2,
                          MoreArgs = list(average = geometric))

data.frame(
  pair               = paste(ht$construct_1, ht$construct_2, sep = " / "),
  DMAR_htmt          = ht$htmt,
  arithmetic_by_hand = unname(arithmetic_by_hand),
  abs_difference     = unname(abs(ht$htmt - arithmetic_by_hand)),
  geometric_HTMT2    = unname(geometric_HTMT2)
)
```

DMAR and the arithmetic hand computation agree to machine precision. The
HTMT2 column is systematically smaller here, which is why reporting which
variant you used is not a formality: with a .85 or .90 decision rule, the
two variants can land on opposite sides for the same data. SIEVER names
the routine (DMAR::htmt) at the point of display; when you report HTMT, say
that it is the arithmetic mean form of Henseler, Ringle, and Sarstedt
(2015), not HTMT2, for exactly this reason.

### AVE: Two Definitions, Both Correct

Average variance extracted (Fornell & Larcker, 1981) has more than one
implementation in circulation. DMAR's `average_variance_extracted()` is
the mean squared standardized loading, which is the definition SIEVER
records with the AVE table (the recorded step names it in the session
script and the Show code panel). Another form in circulation is the sum of
the items'
common factor variances over the sum of their observed variances, which
weights each squared standardized loading by its item's variance, so it
answers a slightly different question. The two columns below differ by up
to a few hundredths; that is a difference of definition, not a
disagreement about arithmetic, and the hand computed columns settle which
definition DMAR implements.

```{r ave}
a <- average_variance_extracted(fit)

lam_cfa <- standardizedSolution(fit)
lam_cfa <- lam_cfa[lam_cfa$op == "=~", ]
mean_sq <- tapply(lam_cfa$est.std, lam_cfa$lhs, function(x) mean(x^2))

est <- lavInspect(fit, "est")
common <- diag(est$lambda %*% est$psi %*% t(est$lambda))
observed <- diag(lavInspect(fit, "sampstat")$cov)
variance_weighted <- sapply(a$factor, function(f) {
  ix <- est$lambda[, f] != 0
  sum(common[ix]) / sum(observed[ix])
})

data.frame(
  factor            = a$factor,
  DMAR_ave          = a$ave,
  mean_sq_loading   = unname(mean_sq[a$factor]),
  abs_difference    = unname(abs(a$ave - mean_sq[a$factor])),
  variance_weighted = unname(variance_weighted)
)
```

DMAR matches the mean squared loading exactly. The variance weighted column
is reported here so that a reader comparing SIEVER's output to a paper that
used the other definition knows immediately why the second decimal moved,
and which definition each number is on.

## Invariants That Must Hold for All Inputs

Fixed comparisons check one dataset. The checks in this section state
properties that must hold for every input, given how each procedure is
built, which is a stronger kind of evidence: if the property fails on any
data, something is wrong.

### A Confidence Interval Widens With Its Confidence Level

A confidence interval for omega built around one estimate with one
standard error, as the delta method interval checked here is, must be
monotone non-decreasing in width as the confidence level rises. That
follows from how the interval is built, not from these data (an interval
recomputed from new random draws at each level need not be nested), and
a routing defect (a confidence level passed to the wrong argument, an
interval built at a fixed level regardless of the request) shows up here
immediately.

```{r ci-monotone}
levels <- c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99)
ints <- t(vapply(levels, function(cl) {
  r <- reliability_omega(data = d[, blocks$Textual], ci_method = "mlr_logistic",
                         denominator = "model_implied", conf_level = cl)
  c(estimate = r$value[r$term == "estimate"],
    lower    = r$value[r$term == "ci_lower"],
    upper    = r$value[r$term == "ci_upper"])
}, numeric(3)))

out <- data.frame(conf_level = levels, ints,
                  width = ints[, "upper"] - ints[, "lower"])
out

c(width_strictly_increasing = all(diff(out$width) > 0),
  estimate_invariant        = length(unique(out$estimate)) == 1L)
```

The widths increase strictly at every step, and the point estimate is
unchanged by the confidence level, as it must be. The interval checked
here is DMAR's default interval of Omega (model-implied denominator), the
MLR (sandwich) standard error with its limits formed on the logit scale,
which SIEVER shows beside its default, Robust omega (observed denominator),
in the compact table, so every construct of continuous items has an
interval in view before any bootstrap is run; robust omega's own interval
is a percentile bootstrap run on request (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit,
2016). For ordered items every interval DMAR gives is a bootstrap, so
their model-implied omega is shown as a point estimate.

**Operating characteristics of the default intervals.** DMAR chose the
logit-scale limits on a Monte Carlo study whose design and decision rule
were written before it ran (DMAR's source repository,
`methodology/reliability_limits`, which the CRAN package does not include):
one-factor models of four and six items and a three-factor model of
three-item factors, N of 50, 100, 200 and 500, and 5,000 replications in
each of 40 cells. With normal data and the normal theory ML standard error,
under complete cases and FIML alike, the logit-scale limits for Omega
(model-implied denominator) covered between .939 and .956 in every one of
the 48 factor by sample size cells, where limits on the scale of omega from
the same standard error covered between .910 and .952, missing mostly below
the lower limit. With nonnormal data (factors and errors from a
standardized chi-square on 4 df) fitted by MLR, the logit-scale limits from
the Huber-White standard error covered between .919 and .951 in 16 factor
by sample size cells, mostly short of .95 because that standard error is
too small at these sizes; the shortfall shrank with N (.936 at N = 200 and
.942 at N = 500 for the six-item factor with loadings .8 to .5). No cell
used the robust.sem standard error the default takes with complete cases.
That study did not include SIEVER's default interval, the percentile
bootstrap of Robust omega (observed denominator).

The
table states, beside every point estimate, the interval, that its
bootstrap has not been run yet (Run the bootstrap, below the table), or
that none is shown (an inadmissible estimate gets no bootstrap).

### The Careless Responding Screens Catch a Constant Responder

The screening tab flags rows, not just items: a respondent who marks the
same option down the whole page distorts every correlation downstream
(Meade & Craig, 2012). Injecting exactly such a row into the bundled data
is a metamorphic check with a known answer, and the screens are SIEVER's
own exported code, `sieve_response_screens()`, the function behind the
Screening tab's Observations panel, so the check exercises that code
rather than a re-derivation of it. The longstring must equal the number of
items, the within person standard deviation must be exactly zero, and the
row must be flagged.

```{r careless}
X <- as.matrix(d)
X <- rbind(X, rep(5, ncol(X)))          # the injected constant responder
injected <- nrow(X)

# SIEVER's rule: a run of at least half the items, rounded up and never
# fewer than two; a missing response breaks the run; the within person SD
# is flagged at or below 0; the Mahalanobis tail is read at p < .001.
scr <- SIEVER::sieve_response_screens(as.data.frame(X))
long_cut <- scr$long_cut

# What the screens measured on the injected row.
scr$tbl[injected, c("longstring", "irv", "p_mahalanobis", "flags", "flagged_by")]

# Whether each screen fires on it.
c(longstring_equals_item_count = scr$tbl$longstring[injected] == ncol(X),
  sd_exactly_zero              = scr$tbl$irv[injected] == 0,
  flagged_longstring           = scr$tbl$longstring[injected] >= long_cut,
  flagged_invariant            = scr$tbl$irv[injected] <= scr$irv_tol,
  flagged_mahalanobis          = scr$tbl$p_mahalanobis[injected] < scr$md_alpha,
  flagged_by_all_three         = scr$tbl$flags[injected] == 3L)
```

All three screens fire on the injected row at once. The complement matters
too: on these continuous ability tests the longstring and invariance
screens should stay quiet, and they do, so the screens are not simply
flagging everything.

```{r careless-complement}
real <- seq_len(nrow(X) - 1L)
c(real_rows_flagged_longstring = sum(scr$tbl$longstring[real] >= long_cut),
  real_rows_flagged_invariant  = sum(scr$tbl$irv[real] <= scr$irv_tol))
```

### Reverse Coding Is an Involution

SIEVER reverse codes an item by reflecting it within its response bounds,
`(min + max) - x`: the bounds declared for it (in its Response bounds cell
in the Ingest tab's item grid, or for several items at once above the
grid, from a file's value labels, or from a specification), or its
observed minimum and maximum when none are declared. Applying that twice must return the
original values exactly, not approximately, because a lossy round trip
would silently corrupt an item every time a user toggled the control off
and on again.

```{r reverse}
reflect <- function(x) (min(x, na.rm = TRUE) + max(x, na.rm = TRUE)) - x

original <- d$t7_sentence
once     <- reflect(original)
twice    <- reflect(once)

c(changed_by_one_pass = !identical(once, original),
  identical_after_two = identical(twice, original))

max(abs(twice - original))    # exact zero, not a small number
```

## Reproducibility: The Seed Contract

SIEVER's seed rule has two halves. A seeded computation must be
reproducible, and a seeded computation must not touch your random number
stream. The second half is the one packages usually get wrong: calling
`set.seed()` inside a function silently reseeds the caller's generator, so
everything the user does afterward changes. SIEVER sets a supplied seed
locally and restores the caller's `.Random.seed` on exit: its own
stochastic code runs under `withr::with_seed()`, and the DMAR routines it
calls receive the seed and seed locally themselves, which the HTMT
bootstrap below demonstrates. With no seed supplied, SIEVER draws one from
your stream (one draw) and records it, so the run can still be replayed.
(Relatedly, no
user facing seed input in the app defaults to a constant: they default to
empty, because a baked-in default makes results look reproducible while
hiding sampling variability from the user.)

The bootstrap upper bound for HTMT is the natural place to demonstrate
both halves.

```{r seeds}
set.seed(1)
before <- .Random.seed

run_1 <- htmt(d, blocks = blocks, B = 200, seed = 1)
run_2 <- htmt(d, blocks = blocks, B = 200, seed = 1)
run_3 <- htmt(d, blocks = blocks, B = 200, seed = 2)

c(same_seed_identical   = identical(run_1$ci_upper, run_2$ci_upper),
  different_seed_differs = !identical(run_1$ci_upper, run_3$ci_upper),
  rng_state_restored     = identical(.Random.seed, before))
```

`identical(.Random.seed, before)` is `TRUE`: byte for byte, the stream is
where you left it, even though three bootstraps of 200 resamples each ran
in between. The seeded runs agree exactly, and a different seed gives
different bounds, which confirms the seed is actually reaching the
resampler rather than being ignored.

```{r seeds-values}
run_1
```

## Re-Running the Evidence Yourself

Everything above is re-runnable in two ways.

* **This vignette.** Its source is `vignettes/validation.Rmd` in the
  package source. Rebuild it with `devtools::build_vignettes()`, or knit
  that file directly. Every number is recomputed at build time.
* **The test suite.** `devtools::test()` runs the same comparisons as
  tests, so a change that broke any of them would fail the suite rather
  than wait for someone to read a vignette.
  `tests/testthat/test-dmar-api-shapes.R` holds the value pinning tests
  against DMAR and the hand derivations, including the bifactor index
  schema, the common method variance identities, the ECVI interval, and
  HTMT seed reproducibility with random number generator restoration.

If you find a quantity SIEVER displays that you cannot reproduce from an
authoritative source, that is a defect worth reporting, and it is the
standard this vignette is written to be held to.
